title: Empiric Antibiotics — Outpatient & Floor Syndromes
sources: Critical Vector — Empiric Therapy Guide Part I: Board-Tested Infections (board-pattern empiric teaching, Aug 2026)
IDSA guidelines: group A strep pharyngitis, uncomplicated UTI, skin & soft-tissue infection, Lyme disease, C. difficile
CDC STI treatment guidelines (2021, ceftriaxone dose increase + doxycycline as chlamydia first-line)

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV Board-Tested Infections guide. Classic triad / signature finding / one empiric regimen, bacterial + fungal + viral. Doses omitted by design; confirm against local resistance patterns.

summary: The outpatient and floor infections with a classic vignette, a signature lab or imaging finding, and one empiric regimen. Companion to the ED/ICU syndromes module. Coverage class shown; doses omitted — confirm against local resistance.

body.text: Bug / drug / why reference for study and clinical reasoning, not an order set. Doses are omitted deliberately. Confirm every regimen against the current guideline and local resistance data before treating a patient.

rows: Group A strep pharyngitis
Penicillin V or amoxicillin (alt: cephalexin, azithromycin if PCN-allergic)
S. pyogenes is universally PCN-sensitive; Centor 3–4 → rapid antigen / culture
Treat to prevent rheumatic fever, not to shorten symptoms. Avoid amoxicillin if mono is on the differential (rash).
CAP — typical, healthy outpatient
Amoxicillin high-dose (alt: doxycycline)
S. pneumoniae dominant; CXR lobar consolidation; CURB-65 to triage site of care
Macrolide monotherapy limited by rising pneumococcal resistance. See the CAP module for inpatient / severe.
CAP — atypical (Mycoplasma / Chlamydophila / Legionella)
Azithromycin or doxycycline
No cell wall / intracellular → beta-lactams ineffective; patchy interstitial infiltrate worse than exam
Legionella triad: hyponatremia + GI symptoms + confusion; urine antigen. Cold agglutinins in Mycoplasma.
Uncomplicated cystitis
Nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMX (alt: single-dose fosfomycin)
Both concentrate in urine with minimal collateral resistance pressure — first-line per stewardship
Avoid nitrofurantoin if early pyelo is suspected (poor tissue penetration) or CrCl < 30.
Pyelonephritis (outpatient-appropriate)
Fluoroquinolone (cipro / levofloxacin) — alt: one dose ceftriaxone → oral step-down
Needs reliable renal-parenchymal and blood-level penetration, unlike nitrofurantoin; WBC casts are specific
Admit for IV therapy if unable to tolerate PO, pregnant, or systemically ill.
Acute otitis media
Amoxicillin high-dose (alt: amox-clavulanate if recent abx or concurrent conjunctivitis)
S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis; high-dose overcomes intermediate pneumococcal resistance
Watchful waiting is appropriate in select low-risk children by age / severity.
Bacterial sinusitis
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Beta-lactamase coverage over amoxicillin addresses H. influenzae / M. catarrhalis co-infection
Criteria: > 10 days without improvement, 'double-worsening', or severe onset with fever > 39 °C + purulent discharge. Most sinusitis is viral.
Bacterial meningitis — neonate
Ampicillin + cefotaxime (or ampicillin + gentamicin)
Ampicillin covers Listeria and GBS (unique to the neonatal period); cefotaxime over ceftriaxone (bilirubin displacement)
Classic neonatal triad: GBS, E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes.
Bacterial meningitis — child / adult
Vancomycin + ceftriaxone + dexamethasone before / with the first dose
Vancomycin for resistant pneumococcus, ceftriaxone for meningococcus + susceptible pneumococcus, steroid blunts hearing loss / mortality in pneumococcal disease
Add ampicillin if age > 50 or immunocompromised (Listeria). Do not delay abx for imaging / LP.
Cellulitis / erysipelas
Cephalexin or dicloxacillin; add TMP-SMX or doxycycline if MRSA risk or purulence
Non-purulent cellulitis is overwhelmingly streptococcal / MSSA — no MRSA spectrum needed absent risk factors
Erysipelas is classically GAS, more superficial / lymphatic, sharply demarcated raised border. Mark the borders to track response.
Lyme disease — early localized
Doxycycline (alt: amoxicillin or cefuroxime in pregnancy / peds)
Borrelia burgdorferi is exquisitely doxy-sensitive; also covers coincident anaplasmosis from the same tick
Clinical diagnosis with erythema migrans in an endemic area. Late disease (carditis, arthritis, neuroborreliosis) escalates to IV ceftriaxone.
Pertussis
Azithromycin
Macrolide reduces transmissibility and shortens the catarrhal phase if given early; marked lymphocytosis on CBC
Largely supportive once the paroxysmal phase is established — antibiotics do not shorten the established cough.
C. difficile colitis
Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (metronidazole only for mild disease / low-resource settings)
Oral vancomycin acts locally in the gut lumen — IV vancomycin does not reach the colon
Fulminant (ileus, megacolon, shock) → oral + rectal vancomycin + IV metronidazole; surgical evaluation.
H. pylori
Bismuth quadruple: PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline (triple PPI + amox + clarithro only if local clarithromycin resistance is low)
Rising clarithromycin resistance shifted first-line to bismuth quadruple in most regions
Confirm eradication with a test-of-cure ≥ 4 weeks after therapy (hold PPI ~2 weeks before testing).
Gonorrhea / chlamydia (cervicitis / urethritis)
Ceftriaxone single IM + doxycycline
Empiric dual coverage for frequent co-infection; ceftriaxone dose raised for gonococcal resistance, doxycycline replaced azithromycin for chlamydia
Treat partners; test for other STIs incl. HIV / syphilis. Disseminated gonococcemia → migratory polyarthralgia + dermatitis.
Syphilis — primary / secondary / early latent
Benzathine penicillin G single IM (late latent / tertiary: weekly × 3)
T. pallidum has no documented penicillin resistance; benzathine maintains treponemicidal levels for weeks
PCN-allergic pregnant patients REQUIRE desensitization — no substitute is acceptable in pregnancy.
Oropharyngeal / esophageal candidiasis
Nystatin swish-and-swallow (mild oral); fluconazole (systemic) for esophageal disease
Esophageal involvement implies deeper mucosal invasion → systemic azole, not topical polyene
Esophageal candidiasis in a young patient is AIDS-defining — check HIV status.
Vulvovaginal candidiasis
Fluconazole single oral dose (alt: topical clotrimazole / miconazole)
Wet mount pseudohyphae; normal vaginal pH < 4.5 distinguishes it from BV / trichomonas
Recurrent disease (≥ 4 / year) warrants evaluation for uncontrolled diabetes.
Invasive candidiasis / candidemia
Echinocandin (micafungin / caspofungin)
Fungicidal, covers azole-resistant Candida (glabrata, auris) — preferred empirically in critically ill patients
Persistent fever despite broad antibacterials in a line-bearing / ICU / TPN patient. Dilated eye exam for endophthalmitis. Remove / exchange lines.
Cryptococcal meningitis
Liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine (induction) → fluconazole consolidation / maintenance
Combination fungicidal induction clears burden faster and cuts mortality vs fluconazole alone; India ink / CrAg positive
Serial therapeutic LPs to manage elevated opening pressure are often as important as the antifungal. Classic host: AIDS, CD4 < 100.
Histoplasmosis — disseminated / severe pulmonary
Liposomal amphotericin B → itraconazole step-down
Amphotericin for rapid fungicidal control; urine / serum Histoplasma antigen most sensitive
Bird / bat droppings, Ohio / Mississippi River valleys. Mild pulmonary disease in immunocompetent hosts is often self-limited.
Coccidioidomycosis — severe / disseminated
Fluconazole or itraconazole; amphotericin B for severe / disseminated / CNS disease or pregnancy
Azole is usually sufficient; amphotericin reserved for severe or CNS disease and pregnancy (azole teratogenicity)
'Valley fever' — Southwestern US dust exposure, erythema nodosum, arthralgias. Most immunocompetent cases are self-limited.
Influenza
Oseltamivir — within 48 h of onset, or any time if hospitalized / high-risk
Neuraminidase inhibition blocks viral release; benefit greatest early in the replication curve
Still indicated later in hospitalized / high-risk patients despite the 48-h window.
HSV — genital / oral
Valacyclovir or acyclovir
Nucleoside analog terminates viral DNA chain elongation via HSV thymidine kinase — shortens outbreaks, reduces shedding, not curative
Daily suppressive therapy reduces transmission and recurrence in frequent recurrers.
HSV encephalitis
IV acyclovir — start empirically, treat before confirmation
Untreated mortality ~70%; low toxicity of a short course justifies empiric use on suspicion
MRI temporal-lobe edema / hemorrhage; CSF HSV PCR (can be falsely negative very early). Start before LP / imaging results return.
VZV — varicella / zoster
Valacyclovir, within 72 h of rash onset
Time-dependent efficacy — only meaningfully effective started early in the vesicular phase
Zoster ophthalmicus (nasociliary involvement, Hutchinson's sign) needs urgent ophthalmology referral.
EBV mononucleosis
Supportive care — no antiviral indicated
Self-limited in immunocompetent hosts; heterophile (Monospot) positive, atypical lymphocytosis, transaminitis
Avoid amoxicillin / ampicillin (near-universal morbilliform rash). Avoid contact sports 3–4 weeks (splenic rupture).
CMV — immunocompromised (retinitis, colitis)
Ganciclovir or valganciclovir PO; foscarnet for ganciclovir-resistant disease
Reserved for end-organ disease where untreated CMV causes irreversible damage (blindness, colitis)
Retinitis in AIDS with CD4 < 50. Immunocompetent CMV mono-like illness is self-limited and needs no treatment.
HIV — acute retroviral syndrome
Refer for prompt ART initiation (regimen per specialist)
Early ART shrinks the reservoir, cuts transmission, improves outcomes — treat regardless of CD4
4th-gen Ag/Ab test (p24 antigen); confirm with HIV RNA if antibody is in the window period. Consider PEP for a high-risk exposure within 72 h.
Hepatitis C
Direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir-based combinations)
DAAs target NS3/4A, NS5A, NS5B → > 95% cure vs interferon-era regimens
Anti-HCV antibody → HCV RNA confirms active infection; genotype guides the regimen. Universal one-time screening for all adults.

items: Narrow first-line agents (penicillin for strep throat, nitrofurantoin for cystitis, cephalexin for non-purulent cellulitis) are chosen for stewardship — reach for broader spectrum only when a specific risk factor is present.
'Treat before confirmation' syndromes: bacterial meningitis, HSV encephalitis, meningococcemia (see the ED/ICU module) — the cost of delay outweighs the cost of empiric therapy.
Avoid aminopenicillins when EBV / infectious mononucleosis is on the differential (rash).
Oral vancomycin — not IV — for C. difficile; the drug has to be in the gut lumen.
Benzathine penicillin is the only acceptable syphilis therapy in pregnancy; a PCN-allergic pregnant patient is desensitized, not switched.
